profile.story: Meridian places light-industrial and administrative contractors — warehouse, assembly, packaging, front office — with about 60 client companies across three metros. Thirty internal staff carry roughly 420 contractors on assignment at any time. It is the largest business in the cohort by revenue and one of the thinnest by margin: gross spread is 18% on the P&L, and Nia has spent years managing the business as though it were 30%. That single number sits underneath every bill rate she has approved, every recruiter incentive she has set and the two-location expansion she is planning. The systems are decent, the team is real, and the arithmetic under the pricing is wrong.

The gap is the finding, not a data-entry error — the intake was completed by her controller from the P&L, and the owner's working number came out of her own mouth in the room
Gate passes; opportunity confidence is medium throughout because pricing decisions rest on a margin the owner does not carry accurately

blockNotes.b1: Q8 belief is bill rates and discounting, and the evidence half agrees — but the reason is not the one she thinks. Objective is profit and then scale into two more metros.
blockNotes.b2: READ WITH THE CROSS-CHECK PANEL. Funnel reconciles cleanly: 90 job orders a month, 42% filled, $16,600 per filled assignment gives $7.53M against $7.50M on the P&L. The margin check will not. Asked for gross margin in the room, Nia said 'about thirty percent' without hesitating — twice, and she used it again later when talking about a bill rate. The P&L on file says 18%, and the intake says 18% because her controller completed that section from the same P&L. This is not a typo and not a bad P&L: the books are clean and prepared by an outside controller. It is the owner carrying a number twelve points wrong, and carrying it into every rate approval, every account manager conversation and the two-market expansion plan. Flag stands; the ask on flag was put to her and her answer was 'thirty is the spread we quote.' Quoted spread before discounting, before unbilled overtime, before workers' comp and before the payroll-only accommodation work is exactly how eighteen becomes thirty in someone's head.
blockNotes.b3: Rate card on file by role and metro, set against competitor rates rather than against loaded cost. Discount rules exist and are written — and by the branch managers' own account the two longest-serving account managers use the bottom of the band as the opening number. Direct hire is 9% of revenue at 84% margin and nobody is targeted on it.
blockNotes.b4: 59 h/wk repetitive against a 30-person, 1,200-hour payroll — 4.9%, well inside the check and no single role overloaded. Candidate-side automation is strong; the client side has almost none, and timesheet chasing alone is 14 hours a week that also delays invoicing by six days.
blockNotes.b5: Largest client 19% on the revenue-by-client report — under the 25% threshold but on a 30-day MSA and concentrated in the newest branch. Contracts, licences and insurance all written, current and transferable. Access review is the weak spot: ex-employee access has never been reviewed.

P1.note: Five order sources with monthly volume in the ATS (q23: repeat 52, outbound 21, referrals 9, inbound 6, portals 2), four of five tracked, cost known only on the $4,200 job board spend.
P1.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs cost or quality tracked for the main source; the main source is client repeat, which carries neither, and referrals are untracked entirely.

P2.note: Every job order lands in the ATS including declined ones (q24), acknowledged inside an hour and sourced the same day — watched live at eleven minutes from order to sourcing.
P2.why_not_higher: Anchor 4 needs the response automated; the acknowledgement is a person, and there is no automated client-side response at all (q45).

P3.note: Candidate-side sequences are effectively universal and automated; on the client side, unfilled orders get a second touch about 60% of the time and it depends on the account manager (q24).
P3.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs a defined sequence with missed follow-ups visible — an unfilled order that goes quiet is not surfaced anywhere in the ATS.

P4.note: Fill rate 42% tracked by recruiter and client in the ATS and reviewed weekly (observed). Loss reasons — speed and rate — are known but recorded informally.
P4.why_not_higher: Q25: for new client acquisition there is no process at all, 'whatever each account manager does', so the tracked process covers only half the motion.

P5.note: Rate card on file by role and metro with written discount rules — but set against competitor rates rather than loaded cost, and the spread-by-client report shows light industrial at 16% against a quoted 30%. The owner's own working margin is twelve points off the P&L (b2).
P5.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs real economics behind the price; the price is set against competitors and defended with a margin number that does not exist, which is the anchor-1 line even though a discount rule is written.

P6.note: Direct hire conversion, screening packages, employer-of-record and a managed on-site programme all exist and are offered when the client asks (q29).
P6.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs a scripted upsell on the core offer; direct hire is 84% margin, nobody is targeted on it, and the premium on-site programme has never been sold to a third client.

P7.note: Placement report measures 78% quarterly reorder and 85% MSA renewal; the ATS can list clients dormant six months and it has been pulled once (q27).
P7.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs the inactive list worked at least twice a year; no reactivation has ever run.

P8.note: Five account managers own territories, the weekly review covers orders, fills and client value by branch with named owners (q30, q39).
P8.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs the value side reviewed monthly by named owners — marketing has no internal owner, acquisition cost is never in the meeting, and no margin number is on the branch boards.

P9.note: The books know: spread by client and assignment is on file and accurate (16% light industrial, 22% administrative, 84% direct hire). The business does not — the owner said 'about thirty percent' twice in the room against 18% on the P&L, and the margin report is rebuilt in Excel monthly by one person (b2, b4).
P9.why_not_higher: The rubric scores what the business runs on, not what its accountant can produce. A margin figure that exists in a monthly spreadsheet and is contradicted by the decision-maker is the 'estimated once a year' line, not 'known overall'.

P10.note: Monthly close inside 15 days with an outside controller, AR aging current, and q21 carries revenue, spread, profit, cash and comp targets.
P10.why_not_higher: Held at 2 rather than 3 because the review demonstrably is not landing: the owner's working margin is twelve points from the statement she receives every month, and invoicing runs six days behind the week close.

S1.note: Branch managers decide inside their branch up to the rate card and the branches genuinely run (q51); q50 keeps rate exceptions, major sales, escalations, hiring, banking and strategy with Nia.
S1.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs decision rights written for most areas; the rate card is the only written boundary and every exception to it is hers.

S2.note: Four-week test (q51): recruiting, placement, payroll, compliance and invoicing all keep running. New client acquisition and rate exceptions stop.
S2.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs a named deputy with a few owner-locked items; there are five branch managers and no one above them, so exceptions stack rather than resolve — and an 8-day absence this year included approving three rates from an airport.

S3.note: Five account managers hold their own territories and close standard business; only about 25% of revenue traces to the owner's three founding relationships (q14), and the live order came in and was worked without her.
S3.why_not_higher: Anchor 4 needs relationships institutional — a quarter of revenue on the owner's personal relationships and every rate exception routing to her keeps this short of it.

S4.note: Five managers with direct reports; each owns their branch's four KPIs and q34 rates accountable ownership 'usually' true.
S4.why_not_higher: Q39 is explicit: nothing on the branch boards is a margin number, so managers own volume and nobody owns profitability — anchor 3 needs managers owning outcomes and metrics that matter.

S5.note: SharePoint library opened in session: onboarding and compliance procedures current and used in training (q35: 55% documented). Rate setting and client acquisition have nothing written.
S5.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs the core workflows documented and current; the two that carry the margin are the two that are missing, and only 45% is actually followed.

S6.note: Weekly structured review observed across three branches with four owned KPIs and visible targets (q39, q40).
S6.why_not_higher: Held at 2 on content rather than form: four volume KPIs with no margin measure means the rhythm is real and is pointed at the wrong number — a margin miss triggers nothing by her own answer.

S7.note: 420 contractors placed and supported consistently; q36 lists incomplete information and missed handoffs as recurring, and q31 says a 20% jump needs hiring.
S7.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs +20% to strain rather than break with QC steps defined; fill rate is already 42% and q37 names sales capacity as the limiting resource, so more orders would lower it.

S8.note: Revenue-by-client report: largest 19%, top five 48% across about 60 billing clients. Under the 25% overlay threshold — a watch item, not a warning — but on a 30-day-notice MSA and concentrated in the newest branch (q52).
S8.why_not_higher: v2 anchor 3 is 10–15%; 19% sits in the 15–20% band.

S9.note: Q12: 58% recurring contract revenue under MSAs renewing at 85%, plus 29% repeat without contract, with 420 contractors on assignment providing a visible forward book in the ATS.
S9.why_not_higher: Anchor 4 needs it genuinely forecastable — MSAs carry 30-day notice and no revenue forecast is produced, so the base is contracted but not planned from.

S10.note: Q53 returns nearly everything true including transferable contracts, and the MSAs, vendor agreements, licences and insurance were all in the data room.
S10.why_not_higher: Q52 names four unaddressed exposures — the 19% client on 30 days' notice, the owner on rate exceptions, the workers' comp experience rating, and a sole billing coordinator. No cross-training and no continuity plan.

L1.note: ATS with a client CRM module, a staffing payroll platform, an onboarding and compliance portal, QuickBooks, SharePoint and Teams cover the core areas (q41).
L1.why_not_higher: One significant gap remains and it is the expensive one: there is no margin reporting system — spread is rebuilt in Excel by hand every month.

L2.note: ATS ↔ payroll platform is connected and works, shown on the tour; q42 'some integrations'.
L2.why_not_higher: Payroll → Excel → QuickBooks is manual every month, timesheets arrive through three separate client portals, and internal and contractor payroll sit in different systems — more than the one or two double-entry points anchor 3 allows.

L3.note: Q43 claims agreed definitions and accurate data, and the volume reporting is genuinely good. But the number the business is priced on is disputed inside the business itself — 18% on the statement, 30% in the owner's head (b2) — and the margin report is hand-built monthly.
L3.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs the numbers mostly right after cleanup; here the headline financial metric is not agreed between the owner and her own P&L, which is the definition of one trusted report and everything else disputed.

L4.note: 59 h/wk inventoried (q44). Candidate-side work has genuinely been reduced by automation; timesheet chasing (14h), invoicing reconciliation (9h) and compliance chasing (8h) are untouched and delay invoicing six days.
L4.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs a few fixes made across the load; every fix so far is on one side of the business and the client side has had none.

L5.note: Application acknowledgements, screening reminders, shift SMS and compliance document requests all run reliably and were shown firing, with the recruiting coordinator monitoring them (q45).
L5.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs automations across several functions; all of these sit in candidate operations and nothing exists in client, billing or reporting.

L6.note: Q46 covers five categories — recruiters use it for job posts and screening summaries, account managers for client emails, the marketing contractor for content.
L6.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs AI inside one or two defined workflows; this is individual use spread across roles with no workflow depending on it and no result recorded.

L7.note: Q47 returns two of eight — someone accountable per implementation and sensitive-data rules defined (driven by candidate PII obligations). No human-review rule, nothing measured, no impact-based selection.
L7.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs several practices however inconsistent; two, one of them purely compliance-driven, is not several — and q48 confirms sensitive data is already going into unapproved tools.

L8.note: Q48: unclear access, ex-employees may retain access, sensitive data in unapproved tools — against q43 confirming backups and a known data map. Partial hygiene with known gaps.
L8.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs access controlled and off-boarding done; in a business holding social security numbers and I-9s for 420 contractors, unreviewed ex-employee access is the specific gap that holds this at 2.

L9.note: Q58 'pockets of capability'; q59 names the Columbus branch manager building her own ATS reports and the billing coordinator as motivated, against two account managers who will resist rate discipline.
L9.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs the team trained on the core tools; no training programme exists and the capability that shows is individual initiative.

L10.note: Q49: $30–50K budget, 5 owner hours and 12 team hours; q55 'ready, with leadership capacity' and five branch managers to carry it.
L10.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs budget and time set aside; the ATS and payroll are explicitly off-limits mid-year by her own answer, which fences the change out of the systems where the work actually is.

assessment.owner_objective: More profit & cash flow — then Prepare to scale, Better operations & delivery capacity
assessment.owner_belief: We are leaving margin on the table on bill rates. We win orders and I think we win too many of them at a number that does not pay us properly, and my account managers discount to keep the client rather than defend the rate. It has been the same story since we opened Toledo two years ago.
assessment.primary_constraint: The business is priced on a margin that does not exist: the owner and her account managers approve bill rates against a 30% spread while the P&L reports 18%, so every rate decision, every discount and the two-market expansion plan rest on a number twelve points wrong — and no margin measure appears on any board, in any meeting, or in any manager's targets.
assessment.constraint_symptoms: The owner stated 30% twice in session against 18% on her own monthly statement; light industrial, 62% of revenue, runs at a 16% spread; the rate card is set against competitors rather than loaded cost; the two longest-serving account managers open at the bottom of the discount band; direct hire at 84% margin is 9% of revenue and nobody is targeted on it; the four weekly KPIs are all volume.
assessment.constraint_cost: ~$225K of gross spread between the 18% achieved and the 21% targeted on $7.5M · ~$29K of billing payroll on 23 weekly hours of timesheet chasing and invoice reconciliation that also delays cash six days · ~$310K sitting past 45 days in AR as a direct consequence of that delay.
assessment.constraint_fix: Rebuild the rate card on loaded cost — wages, taxes, workers' comp, benefits and processing — put realised spread on the weekly branch board next to fill rate, and give branch managers a floor they own rather than an exception they escalate.
assessment.momentum_initiative: Put realised gross spread by branch on the existing weekly board — no new system, no purchase, and it changes what five managers talk about on the first Monday.

Rate card rebuilt on loaded cost with a written branch-level floor — Marcus Vell (controller) — 2026-10-12

Timesheet capture and invoicing automation to cut days-to-invoice from six to two — Renata Diaz (billing coordinator) — 2026-11-16

opportunities.title: Reprice the light-industrial book on loaded cost
opportunities.finding: The spread-by-client report (Doc) shows light industrial — 62% of revenue — running at a 16% spread while the rate card is set against competitor rates rather than loaded cost, and the owner approves against a 30% figure that the P&L does not support (b2). Confidence is medium, not high, for exactly that reason: the pricing decision has been made on the wrong number for long enough that client tolerance for a correction is genuinely unknown. This prices a small, staged move on the light-industrial book only.
opportunities.blueprint: Rate card rebuilt from wages, taxes, workers' comp, benefits and processing cost; a written floor each branch manager owns; new rates on new orders immediately and on existing assignments at their next renewal, largest client last and handled by the owner.
opportunities.replaces: A competitor-matched card defended with a margin that is twelve points optimistic

opportunities.title: Fill more of the orders already accepted
opportunities.finding: 1,080 job orders accepted last year at a 42% fill rate (ATS export, Doc) — roughly $17.9M of order value moving through the business. Q25 names the loss reasons as speed and rate; q24 says unfilled orders get a second touch about 60% of the time and nothing surfaces an order going quiet. Recruiter capacity is real but 22 hours a week of screening is unaugmented.
opportunities.blueprint: Unfilled orders aged and surfaced on the branch board, an automated client-side acknowledgement and status update, and AI-assisted screening summaries so recruiter hours go to candidate conversations rather than to qualification calls.
opportunities.replaces: An unfilled order that quietly stops being anyone's problem

opportunities.title: Stop chasing timesheets by hand
opportunities.finding: Timesheet chasing and invoice reconciliation take 23 hours a week between the payroll team and the billing coordinator (q44; 31 outstanding timesheets across three client portals watched live). It is also the direct cause of a six-day gap between week close and invoice, with $310K of AR past 45 days behind it. Dollarised because the hours come off a billing function that is the constraint on cash conversion, not because payroll would shrink.
opportunities.blueprint: Mobile timesheet capture with automated reminders and client approval, portal submissions pulled rather than re-keyed, and invoicing generated from approved time instead of reconciled in Excel.
opportunities.replaces: A person, three client portals and a phone, every Monday
